HEADLINE: Grant Thornton board mulls new M&A tactics as EY circles
TEXT:
Audit and advisory firm Grant Thornton's board has met to discuss how to handle future takeover approaches, in light of interest from at least two of the big four firms.

It is understood Grant Thornton's board met in Melbourne on Monday and yesterday to discuss potential M&A strategies involving the firm and the past performance of its chief executive Greg Keith in dealing with takeover interest.

It is interesting timing for such a boardroom discussion. It is understood big four consulting firm EY Oceania recently approached Grant Thornton in an effort to explore a takeover, while KPMG was caught taking a look last year.

Sources also said Grant Thornton partners were asked to answer a questionnaire on Keith, as he commences his fourth year in charge. The survey was said to be part of Grant Thornton's corporate governance practices, and include questions pertaining to takeover approaches.

A Grant Thornton spokeswoman told Street Talk yesterday the firm did not comment on the content of board meetings. "We have not met with any firm and we are not in any merger discussions," she said.

An EY spokeswoman declined to comment.

It comes as EY is believed to have made an informal approach to Grant Thornton in a move that would shake up the accounting landscape in Australia.

EY, formerly known as Ernst & Young, is the third-biggest firm by revenue in Australia, posting $1.8 billion in revenue last year.

Grant Thornton is the seventh-biggest firm by revenue in the Financial Review Top 100 Accounting Firms 2018 posting revenue of $255 million last year.

The secret talks were said to have come after KPMG sized up Grant Thornton in late 2018. KPMG never made a formal offer after the two sides had talks about how any potential deal would work.

At the time, Grant Thornton responded to the report in Street Talk by saying the firm had the "largest audit practice outside of the big four" and was "extremely attractive in the marketplace."

The spokeswoman then denied there were any merger plans and said Grant Thornton was "committed to remaining independent to the big four".

HEADLINE: JPMorgan adds four to equities
TEXT:
JPMorgan is bolstering its equities team with four hires, including a senior equities sales trader from Deutsche Bank.

The US bank has hired Mathew Tricks, who will join the firm as a senior sales person in equity distribution.

Tricks spent more than 20 years at Deutsche Bank and will report to JPMorgan co-heads of equities distribution Andrew Tanner and Steve Maartensz.

Tricks will be joined at JPMorgan by fellow Deutsche Bank-er Bob Chen, who will be an analyst in the Wall Street giant's emerging companies team.

JPMorgan has also hired Levi Spry from fund manager JCP Investment Partners to cover mining sector stocks.

And finally, JPMorgan has also hired Alistair Harvey as an analyst in the mining sector, based in Melbourne. He joins JPMorgan from Evolution Mining.

HEADLINE: Gas contractor MPC Kinetic spruiking $500m-plus listing
TEXT:
The IPO roadshow season is in full swing. Hot on the heels of meeting Virgin Australia's Velocity Frequent Flyers, fund managers are meeting coal seam gas services business MPC Kinetic in Melbourne and Sydney this week.

And this one is more of a reacquaintance than a new pitch. It is less than a year ago that MPC Kinetic was last lining up for a run at the ASX boards, and went as far as to host fundies at its George Street, Brisbane, head office and out on site in regional Queensland before the fourth-quarter market rout slammed the IPO window shut.

So with some knowledge about the business, who owns it and why it would want to list, fundies want to know what has happened in the past 12 months.

And, more importantly, whether MPC Kinetic met its forecasts.

It is understood MPC Kinetic has presented some good news on that front. The company told funds in Sydney yesterday that it delivered $60 million in EBITDA for the year to June 30, which was slightly above numbers it provided last November.

The better-than-expected numbers were attributed to growth in its core CSG business, which mostly services big gas operators in the Surat Basin of Queensland. Funds were told MPC Kinetic delivered Australia's two largest pipelines in the year to June 30, which were the 270km Broken Hill drought-proofing pipeline and the 440km Tanami gas pipeline.

Importantly, MPC Kinetic also told funds to expect another 5 per cent to 10 per cent growth at the EBITDA line in the 2020 financial year.

MPC Kinetic is expected to be back in front of funds with formal listing documents post reporting season. Credit Suisse and UBS are overseeing the IPO.

The company is owned by US-based SCF Partners, which is no stranger to listing businesses in the US, and Perth-based Viburnum Funds. The owners are believed to be seeking about a $500 million valuation for the company.

HEADLINE: State Street in $3b-plus shares sales; funds watch for more
TEXT:
State Street Corporation is keeping Australian institutional equities desks on their toes this week.

As the local market hit a record high yesterday, State Street was said to be embarking on one of the biggest share portfolio sales seen in the local market.

Fund managers reckon State Street had offloaded close to $3 billion in ASX-listed stocks by the time the final bell rang yesterday, and there were signs that the selling wasn't over yet.

State Street is believed to be handling the portfolio sale on behalf of third-party clients via its transition management business, which specialises in clearing big licks of stocks to accommodate changes in asset allocation or investment managers.

The identity of the underlying manager or managers is not known - but a few funds out on the street must be under serious pressure, given the size of the transition portfolio. Fund managers reckon UBS's equities desk - the country's biggest institutional equities share trader with about 15 per cent market share - has handled the bulk of the trades with blocks worth more than $2 billion in the past few days.

Those blocks included large lines of Origin Energy ($46.6 million), BHP Billiton ($40 million), Commonwealth Bank of Australia ($35 million), Bapcor ($29 million) and Qantas Airways ($27 million) yesterday, according to IRESS data.

Other brokers involved in selling for State Street are believed to include Goldman Sachs and Citi.

And fund managers were told to expect more of the same in coming days.

Fundies reckon it looks like money flowing from active equity mandates into passive mandates - at what active managers would argue was the worst possible time in the cycle. The market is at record highs, driven by indiscriminate buying across the large cap sector.

That buying is one reason plenty of Australian fund managers have just recorded a horror year.

Most funds underperformed their benchmarks according to Mercer's annual survey.

Mercer found the median manager among 134 strategies measured in the Australian shares category delivered a 9 per cent return before fees, trailing the S&P/ASX 300 Index return of 11.4 per cent in the year ended June 30 and S&P/ASX 200 Index return of 11.5 per cent.

Such performance is sure to have some institutional mandates under review - and perhaps signal more chunky transition portfolios in the weeks ahead.

HEADLINE: 'Broken' Gregg avoids jail for cooking books
TEXT: Former Leighton Holdings chief financial officer Peter Gregg has avoided jail and will likely serve home detention after being found guilty of falsifying the books of the construction group for striking a bogus steel supply deal in 2011. District Court judge Paul Lakatos said Gregg was a "broken man" because the damage to his reputation meant he found it hard to get a job and his second wife had left him after the ASIC brought criminal charges against him. HEADLINE: Directors, proxy firms talk 'go shop' over Dulux
TEXT:
The curtains will close on DuluxGroup's nine-year stint on the ASX boards on Wednesday, when shareholders vote overwhelmingly in favour of a $4.2 billion bid from Japan's Nippon Paint.

It is understood proxy votes heading into the meeting were well and truly enough to see the vote carried - and set in motion DuluxGroup's final week as a listed company.

And while shareholders like the look of the $9.80 a share offer, there was one issue in proxy reports likely to cause some debate inside boardrooms, investment banks and corporate law firms.

Leading proxy firm ISS questioned whether DuluxGroup, its bankers at Macquarie Capital and lawyers at Gilbert + Tobin could have negotiated formal provisions to proactively seek a higher offer after signing of the deal.

"Some shareholders may, however, be concerned that the transaction structure did not provided for a 'Go Shop Period', in which the company and its advisers could effectively conduct an auction process to provide shareholders with market-based evidence whether the Nippon Paint deal does, in fact, represent the best available alternative," ISS said in its report, which recommended clients vote for the deal.

The whole "go shop" issue reared its head at MYOB late last year, when MYOB's board agreed to accept KKR & Co's lowered offer on the provision it could send its bankers out to test appetite of other potential buyers.

While no higher offer could be found, MYOB shareholders ended up accepting KKR's offer on the belief that all other options had been tested. While it was a rollercoaster ride, shareholders seemed happy enough at the end of the day.

DuluxGroup's deal has unfolded quite differently.

Strategic buyer Nippon Paint turned up with a a big offer on a confidential basis, was granted due diligence and followed through with a binding bid. DuluxGroup accepted the offer and entered into a scheme of arrangement.

While DuluxGroup's directors would've been bound to consider any subsequent bids, the difference is that its advisers were not sent shopping for a higher offer.

DuluxGroup would argue such a "go shop" wasn't necessary. Paint is a reasonably small industry globally and the company and its bankers were well aware of the big players and what they might or might not be willing to pay.

And it would also argue that Nippon's offer was a knockout at 16.1 times EBITDA - which is higher than any other M&A deal in the sector globally. Nippon also didn't have a pre-bid stake - unlike KKR at MYOB.

Still, ISS would likely argue there is no harm in sending your bankers searching, just in case. And its view is worth at least considering at a time when there is much scrutiny on directors' duties.

HEADLINE: Hartzer pushes back on lending, NZ squeeze
TEXT: Westpac chief executive Brian Hartzer has accused overzealous regulators of risking economic growth by crimping the bank's ability to lend to households and businesses. Mr Hartzer also warned, in a speech yesterday, that the New Zealand central bank's proposals to increase capital requirements on financial institutions could spark a retreat by Australian banks. He called for an overhaul of property-related taxes to help restore growth in the housing market. Companies p13

HEADLINE: Telstra-NBN row erupts
TEXT:
Telstra boss Andy Penn and NBN Co chief executive Stephen Rue have clashed over the NBN's pricing, bringing to a head long-simmering tensions between the two giants of Australian telecommunications.

Mr Penn has called on NBN Co to slash its wholesale prices, warning the $50 billion network risks being stranded as customers and retailers abandon it for cheaper wireless alternatives.

His comments in a blog post yesterday come as Mr Rue vigorously defends NBN's pricing in an opinion piece in The Australian Financial Review today.

Mr Penn claimed on current settings, an average NBN connection was set to soar in price by as much as $10 a month as consumers demanded more and more data and bandwidth. He proposed NBN Co slash its average wholesale price by nearly $20 to $35 a month.

"An industry where wholesale prices result in zero margins for the downstream retail providers is unsustainable. It will result in higher retail prices, reduced competition and retail providers looking for ways to bypass the NBN altogether - which is bad for customers and bad for the industry," Mr Penn wrote in a blog post.

"This ultimately means fewer customers will connect to the NBN and an increasing number of customers will switch away - undermining the potential social and economic benefits the investment in the network was designed to deliver."

Mr Rue dismissed claims the NBN was unsustainable, saying calls for such a radical price cut ignored the government requirement for the broadband network to pay for itself.

"It doesn't surprise me that as the telecoms industry heads into financial results season, NBN's wholesale pricing plans have been cast in the spotlight once again. Further, what retailer, regardless of industry, doesn't want to get cheaper services from their wholesaler?" Mr Rue writes in the Financial Review today.

Mr Rue dismissed a Link Economics study quoted by Mr Penn that found broadband prices in Australia were among the highest in the world. He said an Alpha Beta study commissioned by NBN Co found that out of 22 countries, prices in Australia were seventh most affordable.

In an explicit dig at Telstra, Mr Rue said billions of dollars of NBN revenue went in payments to the telco giant, having "an obvious impact on wholesale prices".

"Let's not forget that the sum of all NBN payments to Telstra was around $2 billion this year. Our corporate plan points to a continuing payment to Telstra for access to ducts, dark fibre and facilities of $1 billion annually from FY21, representing 20 per cent of forecast revenues, and continuing for decades after the build is completed," he said.

The clash of the two telco titans comes a month after NBN Co launched a wholesale pricing review, asking retailers for feedback on its current pricing structures.

As by far the biggest NBN retailer, accounting for 50 per cent of the market, Telstra's views will hold sway with NBN Co. However, Mr Penn did not deal with the likelihood, as predicted by analysts, that such a major price reduction would almost certainly undermine NBN Co's business model resulting in a multibillion-dollar write-down.

The wholesale price for NBN Co's most popular 50 megabit per second plan is $45 a month. But Mr Penn said increased demand for data would see this rise to $52 to $55 a month.

He said this would happen without any formal change to NBN Co's current pricing structure, thanks to its practice of charging separately for bandwidth through the so-called "Connectivity Virtual Circuit" (CVC) charge.

NBN Co had answered retailer complaints about the CVC charge last year by introducing bundled packages that included a set amount of bandwidth at a flat fee. But Mr Penn said this was not enough, and that increased demand for data would force retailers to spend more on extra CVC.

"To avoid these outcomes, fundamental changes to the pricing framework are required - as opposed to incremental improvements," Mr Penn said. "The primary solution is for NBN to simplify its pricing construct by removing the separate CVC pricing charge, with Telstra proposing a one-part pricing construct to replace the existing 'legacy' and bundle pricing.

"Under the current price constructs, predicted growth in data use will significantly increase the effective per customer price over the next three years. In the case of the bundles, growth in CVC overage will increase the effective price per customer between $5 and $10."

He also called for NBN Co to cut the cost of its higher speed plans, and to offer $10 a month voice-only plans to replace the 12 Mbps plans it now offers.

HEADLINE: Integrity watchdog to probe Crown claims
TEXT:
The Morrison government has ordered an inquiry into the allegations surrounding Crown Resorts, after revelations about its alleged links to money laundering and the federal government's fast-tracking of visas for the casino's Chinese high rollers. Attorney-General Christian Porter has referred the allegations to the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity, which will primarily investigate if federal officials did the wrong thing in their dealings with Crown. HEADLINE: Profits season to test sharemarket's record high
TEXT:
Interest rates drove the Australian sharemarket to a fresh record yesterday, completing an 11½-year journey, but it will take improved corporate earnings to sustain prices at these levels.

A 19.3 point, or 0.3 per cent, advance in the S&P/ASX 200 Index enabled the market to finally surpass its November 1, 2007, high of 6828.7 for a new record close of 6845.1.

Falling bond yields have underpinned interest in global equities this year as alternative avenues of income dry up. That has forced a rethink about whether shares are appropriately valued, and what kind of return is acceptable from stocks when the Australian cash rate is 1 per cent and the US readies to cut rates this week for the first time since 2008.

"The overwhelming influence really is low interest rates, which makes the stockmarket look relatively attractive, even though in historical terms valuations look relatively expensive," said Airlie Funds Management founder John Sevior.

"You could look at valuations relative to recent and past history and say, at face value, a lot of sectors and a lot of stocks look expensive."

The 2018-19 earnings season beginning next week will be the immediate test for shares, given that it comes against a weakening economic backdrop that has compelled the Reserve Bank to cut rates twice in two months, and warn more will follow if needed.

"The most notable fact about the new highs in the Australian stockmarket is that it has taken so long," said Regal Funds Management founder Phil King. After the ASX 200 was created in 1992 it hit records in 13 of its first 15 years, he said.

"Stockmarkets tend to go up over time, something Australians have not had the benefit of over the last 10 years. We certainly think the market trends higher over the next few years, with our largest exposures in sectors such as technology that are not dependent on a weak Australian economy."

The market had flirted with a record close on Monday, before a late slump saw it fall just three points shy. A strong performance at the open on Tuesday blasted the longstanding record, as well as the market's previous intraday high, within the first 10 minutes of trading. The new intraday record is 6875.5 points.

Slowing economic conditions mean the market has ascribed a greater premium to stocks with quality and growth properties.

"The better businesses as a result of their strong market positions and good management tend to find a way to do well, even in difficult environments," Mr Sevior said. "The weaker businesses struggle to get out of their own way."

Materials stocks will be the biggest sources of earnings growth in the upcoming reporting season. According to Morgan Stanley, the market is poised to deliver just 1.6 per cent growth in 2018-19, down from 8.8 per cent 12 months ago. And the broker thinks the 9.8 per cent growth the market is counting on for 2019-20 will be downgraded to low single-digits.

Broad-based optimism across most sectors has propelled the market higher, although gold miners were particularly strong, advancing ahead of the US Federal Reserve's rate decision due on Thursday morning (AEST).

The market has been rallying since late January, when the Fed signalled it was done raising interest rates on the heels of a savage December quarter for shares.

A surprise federal election result and a better-than-expected outcome from the banking royal commission added to interest in Australian shares as bond yields kept sinking.

"The market trades off two fears. One fear is the fear of losing money, and the other fear is the fear of missing out," said Daniel Moore from Investors Mutual.

"A lot of investors have been under-invested post-GFC, and I think this bull market's been quite unpopular. You're definitely starting to see in more recent times a fear of missing out. That's been driven by low interest rates and the expectation of lower rates again."

The yield on the 10-year Australian government bond fell to 1.204 per cent on Tuesday. The Reserve Bank cash rate could fall as low as 0.5 per cent next year, and potentially stay there for an extended period, some economists predict.

Mr Moore said it was not just professional investors participating in this bull market, but financial investors such as institutions and insurance companies increasing their equity allocation.

"You've got to be well aware that while interest rates are 1 per cent and that's supportive for valuations, they're 1 per cent for a reason," the Investors Mutual fund manager said. "We are late cycle and risks within the economy are elevated globally. You have to be very selective. now is not the time for blind optimism."

The US quarterly earnings season has delivered some shocks already, with stocks such as Netflix disappointing on user growth.

"I suspect a significant peak in major global indexes is imminent," warned Justin Braitling from Watermark Funds Management. "The internal health of this bull market has deteriorated in recent weeks, with the leadership narrowing to technology and certain defensive sectors.

"Cyclicals, mid and small cap indexes offshore look like they may have peaked already."

He argued that there is insufficient fuel in the tank to propel the market higher. "My call is we see a major top in the weeks ahead, before we see a repeat of last year's sell-off in the second-half." The fund manager prefers defensives, cash and gold.

You have to be very selective. now is not the time for blind optimism. Daniel Moore, Investors Mutual
